questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the RIGHT TO EQUALITY (Articles 14-18). 1. Article 14 applies to both citizens and non-citizens. 2. Article 15 prohibits discrimination against 'any person' on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. 3. Article 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment) is available only to citizens. 4. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and is enforceable against both the State and private individuals. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.option_text: 1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
All four statements

questions.explanation: Statement 2 is WRONG — Article 15's protection is given to 'any CITIZEN', NOT 'any person' (that wider language appears in Art. 14). Statement 1 is correct (Art. 14 protects 'any person'). Statement 3 is correct (Art. 16 is citizen-only). Statement 4 is correct — Art. 17 runs against both State and private actors (horizontal application, enforced via the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: ASSERTION (A): The writ of Habeas Corpus lies even against private individuals. REASON (R): It is a remedy against unlawful detention, regardless of who is detaining. Which is correct?

options.option_text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Habeas Corpus (produce the body) is UNIQUE among the five writs — it lies against BOTH the State and private individuals. The reason given is exactly the doctrinal rationale: its purpose is freedom from any illegal detention. The other four writs (Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto) lie only against public authorities.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Match List-I (Fundamental Right) with List-II (seminal case). List-I: A. Right to privacy recognised as part of Article 21. B. Doctrine of 'basic structure' laid down. C. 'Procedure established by law' expanded to 'due process'. D. Right to free legal aid read into Article 21. List-II: 1. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). 2. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). 3. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). 4. Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).
questions.explanation: Puttaswamy (2017) — privacy as Art. 21 right (9-judge bench). Kesavananda (1973) — basic-structure doctrine, 13-judge. Maneka Gandhi (1978) — 'procedure established by law' read as fair-just-reasonable, importing due process. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) — legal aid and speedy trial as part of Art. 21. These four cases anchor modern Art. 21 jurisprudence.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following Fundamental Rights is NOT available to non-citizens?

options.option_text: Article 21 — protection of life and personal liberty
Article 20 — protection in respect of conviction for offences
Article 19 — six freedoms (speech, assembly, movement, etc.)
Article 14 — equality before law

questions.explanation: Article 19's six freedoms are available ONLY to citizens (and only to natural persons, not corporations per Bennett Coleman). Articles 14, 20, 21 protect 'any person' — including foreigners. Article 15 (like 16) is also citizen-only. Negative-stem trap: the student must remember which are 'any person' vs 'any citizen'.

questions.stem: Arrange the following events in the evolution of the Right to Property in correct chronological order. 1. 44th Amendment removed Right to Property from Part III. 2. 1st Amendment inserted Art. 31A and 9th Schedule to protect land-reform laws. 3. Kesavananda Bharati held 'basic structure' binds even 42nd-era amendments. 4. Minerva Mills struck down clauses of 42nd Amendment that barred judicial review.
questions.explanation: 1st Amendment = 1951 (land reforms). Kesavananda = 1973 (basic structure). 44th Amendment = 1978 (property demoted to a legal right under Art. 300A). Minerva Mills = 1980 (reaffirmed judicial review as basic structure). Sequence: 1951 → 1973 → 1978 → 1980. Chronological-ordering pattern.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A law made by Parliament authorises preventive detention for up to 4 months without advisory-board review. Which of the following is correct?

options.option_text: The law is valid; Art. 22 permits up to 3 months without review and Parliament may extend
The law is invalid; Art. 22(4) caps detention beyond 3 months unless an Advisory Board recommends extension
The law is valid only during a National Emergency
The law is valid only for foreigners

questions.explanation: Article 22(4) is strict: no preventive-detention law shall authorise detention for a period longer than THREE months unless an Advisory Board (of High Court Judges-qualified persons) reports sufficient cause within that period. A 4-month-no-review law violates this cap. Not dependent on Emergency or citizenship. 44th Amendment tried to reduce 3 months to 2 but that provision was not brought into force.

questions.stem: Consider the following FRs and the ground on which the State may restrict them. Which pairing is INCORRECT?

options.option_text: Art. 19(1)(a) freedom of speech — 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground
Art. 19(1)(d) freedom of movement — 'interest of any Scheduled Tribe' as a ground
Art. 19(1)(g) freedom of profession — 'public interest' as a ground
Art. 25 freedom of religion — 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground

questions.explanation: Art. 25 permits reasonable restrictions only on grounds of PUBLIC ORDER, MORALITY, HEALTH and OTHER PROVISIONS OF PART III. 'Sovereignty and integrity of India' is a ground for Art. 19(1)(a)/(b)/(c)/(d) (added by 16th Amendment, 1963), not for Art. 25. All other pairings in the question are correct. Negative-stem pattern.

questions.stem: ASSERTION (A): During a Proclamation of Emergency under Art. 352, all Fundamental Rights stand suspended. REASON (R): Art. 359 empowers the President to suspend the right to move any court for enforcement of FRs specified in the order.

options.option_text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false

questions.explanation: A is FALSE: post 44th Amendment (1978), Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended, even during Emergency. R is TRUE: Art. 359 lets the President suspend ENFORCEMENT of specified FRs (not the rights themselves, and not 20/21). The trap is the word 'all' in A — a single counter-example falsifies it.
